LECTURE 25 Stage 5: Pretraining

Evaluating Generative Text Models

Cross-Entropy Loss, Perplexity, and Measuring How Well a Model Predicts Language
45 min read Advanced Quantifying model quality before, during, and after pretraining

Introduction: Why We Need Metrics for Language Models

We have now built every component of a GPT-style Transformer — token embeddings, positional encodings, multi-head causal self-attention, feed-forward networks with GELU activation, layer normalization, residual connections, and full Transformer blocks stacked into a complete model. But before we can train this model, we need to answer a fundamental question: how do we know if the model is getting better?

Unlike classification tasks where accuracy gives a clear answer ("you got 92% of labels correct"), generative language models pose a subtler challenge. The model outputs a probability distribution over the entire vocabulary at every position in a sequence. It does not just pick one word — it assigns probabilities to all possible next tokens. We need metrics that capture how good these probability distributions are.

The Core Idea: A perfect language model would assign probability 1.0 to whichever token actually comes next, and 0.0 to every other token. A terrible model would spread probability uniformly across the vocabulary, essentially guessing randomly. Our metrics measure where on this spectrum a model falls.

In this lecture, we build two foundational metrics from scratch: cross-entropy loss (the function we minimize during training) and perplexity (the intuitive evaluation metric derived from it). These are not merely abstract formulas — they are the compass that guides every decision about learning rate, batch size, model size, and training duration during pretraining.

From Probabilities to Loss: The Cross-Entropy Story

What the Model Actually Outputs

Recall that our GPT model ends with a linear projection from the hidden dimension (d_model) to the vocabulary size (vocab_size). For a vocabulary of 50,257 tokens (GPT-2), each position produces a vector of 50,257 numbers called logits. These are raw, unnormalized scores — any real number, positive or negative.

To convert logits into probabilities, we apply the softmax function:

Softmax Function

P(token = i) = exp(zi) / ∑j=1V exp(zj)

This guarantees all probabilities are positive and sum to 1. Higher logits correspond to higher probabilities. The softmax is "soft" because it gives some probability to every token, with the distribution becoming more peaked as logit differences grow.

The Cross-Entropy Loss Function

Suppose the model predicts probability P(token = i) for each token, and the actual next token is token t. The cross-entropy loss measures how surprised the model was by the true token:

Cross-Entropy Loss (Single Token)

L = −log P(token = t)

This is simply the negative log-probability of the correct answer.

Why this formula makes intuitive sense:

  • Probability 1.0 for correct token: L = −log(1.0) = 0. Perfect prediction, zero loss.
  • Probability 0.5: L = −log(0.5) ≈ 0.693. Decent but uncertain.
  • Probability 0.01: L = −log(0.01) ≈ 4.605. Very surprised by the correct token.
  • Probability approaching 0: L → ∞. Catastrophically wrong.
Analogy: The Weather Forecaster

Imagine a weather forecaster who assigns probabilities to tomorrow's weather. If they say "90% chance of rain" and it rains, their loss is low (−log(0.9) ≈ 0.105). If they say "5% chance of rain" and it rains, their loss is very high (−log(0.05) ≈ 3.0). Cross-entropy penalizes confident wrong predictions much more severely than uncertain ones. This is exactly what we want: a model that says "I'm 99% sure the next word is 'cat'" and turns out to be wrong should receive a huge penalty.

The LogSoftmax Trick for Numerical Stability

In practice, we never explicitly compute softmax probabilities and then take the log. Instead, we use the log-softmax identity, which is more numerically stable:

Log-Softmax (Numerically Stable)

log P(token = i) = (zi − zmax) − log(∑j=1V exp(zj − zmax))

By subtracting the maximum logit before exponentiating, we avoid computing exp of very large numbers (which would overflow to infinity). The subtraction cancels out mathematically but prevents numerical catastrophe.

For a complete sequence of T tokens, we compute the loss at each position and average. Each term measures how well the model predicted the token at position i given all preceding tokens:

Lseq = −(1/T) ∑i=1T log P(tokeni | token1, ..., tokeni−1)

Python 

import numpy as np
np.random.seed(42)

# ============================================================
# Cross-Entropy Loss from Scratch
# ============================================================

def softmax(logits):
    """Compute softmax probabilities (numerically stable)."""
    shifted = logits - np.max(logits, axis=-1, keepdims=True)
    exp_vals = np.exp(shifted)
    return exp_vals / np.sum(exp_vals, axis=-1, keepdims=True)

def cross_entropy_loss(logits, targets):
    """
    Compute cross-entropy loss from logits and integer targets.

    logits: (batch_size, seq_len, vocab_size) - raw model outputs
    targets: (batch_size, seq_len) - correct next token IDs
    Returns: scalar average loss
    """
    batch_size, seq_len, vocab_size = logits.shape

    # Log-softmax (numerically stable)
    shifted = logits - np.max(logits, axis=-1, keepdims=True)
    log_sum_exp = np.log(np.sum(np.exp(shifted), axis=-1))
    log_probs = shifted - log_sum_exp[..., np.newaxis]

    # Extract log-probability of the correct token at each position
    batch_idx = np.arange(batch_size)[:, np.newaxis]
    seq_idx = np.arange(seq_len)[np.newaxis, :]
    target_log_probs = log_probs[batch_idx, seq_idx, targets]

    return -np.mean(target_log_probs)

# --- Demo: Three scenarios ---
vocab_size, seq_len, batch_size = 10, 5, 2
logits = np.random.randn(batch_size, seq_len, vocab_size)
targets = np.random.randint(0, vocab_size, (batch_size, seq_len))

loss = cross_entropy_loss(logits, targets)
print("=== Cross-Entropy Loss Demo ===")
print(f"Vocabulary size: {vocab_size} | Sequence length: {seq_len}")
print(f"Random model loss: {loss:.4f}")
print(f"Expected for random guessing: -log(1/{vocab_size}) = {-np.log(1/vocab_size):.4f}")
print()

# Near-perfect model: high logit for correct token
perfect = np.full((batch_size, seq_len, vocab_size), -10.0)
for b in range(batch_size):
    for t in range(seq_len):
        perfect[b, t, targets[b, t]] = 10.0
print(f"Near-perfect model loss: {cross_entropy_loss(perfect, targets):.6f}")
print("  (Close to 0: the model is confident about the right answers)")

# Deliberately wrong model: high logit for wrong tokens
wrong = np.full((batch_size, seq_len, vocab_size), 10.0)
for b in range(batch_size):
    for t in range(seq_len):
        wrong[b, t, targets[b, t]] = -10.0
print(f"Deliberately wrong loss: {cross_entropy_loss(wrong, targets):.4f}")
print("  (Very high: the model is confident about wrong answers)")

Perplexity: Making Loss Intuitive

Cross-entropy loss is the number we optimize, but it is hard to interpret directly. What does a loss of 3.2 really mean? Is that good or bad? This is where perplexity comes in — it converts the abstract loss value into something you can grasp intuitively.

Perplexity

PPL = exp(L)

where L is the average cross-entropy loss per token. Perplexity represents the effective number of tokens the model is choosing between at each step. If a model has perplexity 100, it means the model is, on average, as uncertain as if it were choosing uniformly among 100 equally likely tokens.

Lower perplexity always means a better model. Here are reference points:

  • PPL = 1: Perfect prediction. The model always knows exactly what comes next.
  • PPL = vocab_size (e.g., 50,257): Random guessing. The model has learned nothing.
  • GPT-2 Small: PPL ~35 on WikiText-103 — narrowing down to ~35 plausible next tokens.
  • GPT-3 (175B): PPL ~20 on similar benchmarks.
  • State-of-the-art (2024-2025): Perplexities in the low teens.
Analogy: The Multiple-Choice Test

Imagine taking a test where each question has V answer choices. Perplexity tells you the effective number of choices the model thinks are plausible. A perplexity of 5 means the model has narrowed it down to about 5 plausible choices, even if V is 50,000. A perplexity of 50,000 means all tokens look equally likely — the model has learned nothing about the structure of language.

Why Perplexity Is Ideal for Comparing Models

Perplexity has several properties that make it the standard evaluation metric:

  1. Scale-invariant: PPL of 20 means the same thing regardless of vocabulary size or dataset size.
  2. Multiplicative: Halving the perplexity (e.g., 40 to 20) means the model has doubled its predictive precision.
  3. Comparable: You can directly compare PPL between architectures (same vocab and eval set).
  4. Lower is better: Simple, unambiguous interpretation.
Python 

import numpy as np
np.random.seed(42)

# ============================================================
# Perplexity: From Loss to Intuition
# ============================================================

def compute_perplexity(logits, targets):
    """Compute both cross-entropy loss and perplexity."""
    batch_size, seq_len, vocab_size = logits.shape
    shifted = logits - np.max(logits, axis=-1, keepdims=True)
    log_sum_exp = np.log(np.sum(np.exp(shifted), axis=-1))
    log_probs = shifted - log_sum_exp[..., np.newaxis]
    batch_idx = np.arange(batch_size)[:, np.newaxis]
    seq_idx = np.arange(seq_len)[np.newaxis, :]
    target_log_probs = log_probs[batch_idx, seq_idx, targets]
    avg_loss = -np.mean(target_log_probs)
    return avg_loss, np.exp(avg_loss)

# Simulate models at different quality levels
vocab_size, seq_len, batch_size = 1000, 50, 4
targets = np.random.randint(0, vocab_size, (batch_size, seq_len))

print("=== Perplexity at Different Model Quality Levels ===")
print(f"Vocabulary size: {vocab_size}")
print()
print(f"{'Model Quality':<22} {'Loss':>7} {'Perplexity':>11} {'Interpretation'}")
print("-" * 75)

configs = [
    ("Random (untrained)", 0.01, 0.0),
    ("Slightly trained",   0.5,  2.0),
    ("Moderately trained", 0.3,  4.0),
    ("Well-trained",       0.2,  6.0),
    ("Excellent",          0.1, 10.0),
]
for name, noise_scale, boost in configs:
    logits = np.random.randn(batch_size, seq_len, vocab_size) * noise_scale
    if boost > 0:
        for b in range(batch_size):
            for t in range(seq_len):
                logits[b, t, targets[b, t]] += boost
    loss, ppl = compute_perplexity(logits, targets)
    print(f"  {name:<20} {loss:>7.3f} {ppl:>11.1f}   Choosing among ~{ppl:.0f} tokens")

print()
print("Key insight: As the model improves, perplexity drops from ~1000")
print("(random guessing across 1000 tokens) toward single digits.")
print("Each improvement means the model is more 'certain' about what comes next.")

Training vs. Validation Loss: Detecting Overfitting

In practice, we never just look at a single loss number. We compute loss on two separate datasets:

  • Training loss: Computed on data the model has seen and learned from. This should always decrease.
  • Validation loss: Computed on data the model has never seen. This reveals whether the model is learning general patterns or just memorizing the training data.

The Overfitting Signal

The relationship between training and validation loss reveals three training regimes:

  • Underfitting: Both losses are high. The model has not learned enough. Keep training.
  • Good fit: Both losses are low and close together. The model has learned generalizable patterns.
  • Overfitting: Training loss keeps decreasing but validation loss starts increasing. The model is memorizing.

The gap between validation and training loss is called the generalization gap. A growing gap is the clearest signal that overfitting has begun.

Token-Level vs. Sequence-Level Metrics

There is an important distinction worth understanding:

  • Token-level metrics (loss, perplexity per token): Used during pretraining. They provide a smooth, differentiable signal for the optimizer.
  • Sequence-level metrics (BLEU, ROUGE, human evaluation): Evaluate complete generated sequences. Reserved for downstream task evaluation after pretraining.
Python 

import numpy as np
np.random.seed(42)

# ============================================================
# Simulating Training vs Validation Loss Over Training
# ============================================================

n_epochs = 50
epochs = np.arange(1, n_epochs + 1)

# Training loss: always decreasing (with noise)
train_loss = 8.0 * np.exp(-0.08 * epochs) + 0.5 + np.random.randn(n_epochs) * 0.05

# Validation loss: decreases, then increases (overfitting after epoch ~30)
val_loss = 8.0 * np.exp(-0.06 * epochs) + 0.7
val_loss[epochs > 30] += 0.03 * (epochs[epochs > 30] - 30) ** 1.2
val_loss += np.random.randn(n_epochs) * 0.08

best_epoch = np.argmin(val_loss) + 1
best_val = val_loss[best_epoch - 1]

print("=== Training vs Validation Loss ===")
print()
print(f"{'Epoch':>5} {'Train Loss':>10} {'Val Loss':>10} {'Gap':>7} {'Status'}")
print("-" * 58)
for i in range(0, n_epochs, 5):
    e, tl, vl = epochs[i], train_loss[i], val_loss[i]
    gap = vl - tl
    if e < 15:
        status = "Underfitting (both high)"
    elif e <= 35:
        status = "Good fit"
    else:
        status = "OVERFITTING!"
    marker = " <-- BEST" if abs(e - best_epoch) < 3 else ""
    print(f"  {e:3d}    {tl:7.3f}    {vl:7.3f}  {gap:+6.3f}  {status}{marker}")

print(f"\
Best validation loss: {best_val:.3f} at epoch {best_epoch}")
print(f"Generalization gap at best epoch: {best_val - train_loss[best_epoch-1]:.3f}")

# ASCII plot of training curves
print("\
=== Loss Curves (ASCII Plot) ===\
")
height, width = 18, 50
y_min = min(min(train_loss), min(val_loss)) - 0.1
y_max = max(max(train_loss), max(val_loss)) + 0.1
grid = [[' '] * width for _ in range(height)]
for i in range(n_epochs):
    x = int((i / (n_epochs - 1)) * (width - 1))
    for arr, ch in [(train_loss, 'T'), (val_loss, 'V')]:
        y = int((1 - (arr[i] - y_min) / (y_max - y_min)) * (height - 1))
        y = max(0, min(height - 1, y))
        grid[y][x] = ch if grid[y][x] == ' ' else 'X'
for r_i, row in enumerate(grid):
    lv = y_max - (r_i / (height - 1)) * (y_max - y_min)
    print(f"  {lv:5.2f} |{''.join(row)}|")
print(f"        {''.join(['-'] * width)}")
print(f"        Epoch 1{' ' * (width - 12)}Epoch {n_epochs}")
print(f"        T = Training Loss   V = Validation Loss   X = Overlap")
print()
print("Notice how T keeps dropping while V curves upward after epoch ~30.")
print("This divergence is the classic overfitting signature.")

The Loss Landscape: Visualizing What the Optimizer Sees

When we train a model, the optimizer navigates a high-dimensional loss landscape — a surface where each point corresponds to a particular set of model weights, and the height is the loss value. Understanding key features of this landscape builds crucial intuition:

  • Global minimum: The absolute lowest point. Finding this is generally impossible for neural networks.
  • Local minima: Points lower than their immediate neighbors. For large models, these are often "good enough" — research shows they tend to have similar loss values.
  • Saddle points: Minima in some directions, maxima in others. More common than local minima in high dimensions and can slow training significantly.
  • Flat regions (plateaus): Large areas where the loss barely changes. Gradients are near zero, making progress painfully slow.

Research has shown that larger models tend to have smoother, better-behaved landscapes with fewer problematic local minima. This is one reason why scaling up model size often makes training easier, not harder — a counterintuitive but well-documented finding.

Python 

import numpy as np
np.random.seed(42)

# ============================================================
# Visualizing a 2D Loss Landscape with Gradient Descent
# ============================================================

def loss_fn(x, y):
    """A synthetic 2D loss landscape with interesting features."""
    return (2.0 * np.sin(0.5*x) * np.cos(0.3*y)
            + 0.5 * (x-1)**2 + 0.3 * (y+0.5)**2
            - 1.5 * np.exp(-((x+2)**2 + (y-2)**2) / 1.5)
            + 0.3 * np.sin(2*x) * np.sin(2*y))

# Create ASCII landscape
x_r = np.linspace(-4, 4, 40)
y_r = np.linspace(-4, 4, 22)
X, Y = np.meshgrid(x_r, y_r)
Z = loss_fn(X, Y)
Z_norm = (Z - Z.min()) / (Z.max() - Z.min())
chars = ' .:-=+*#%@'

print("=== 2D Loss Landscape ===")
print("Each character represents the loss at that point in weight space.")
print("Light/sparse = low loss (valleys), dark/dense = high loss (peaks)\
")

for i in range(len(y_r)-1, -1, -1):
    row = ''
    for j in range(len(x_r)):
        level = int(Z_norm[i, j] * (len(chars) - 1))
        level = max(0, min(len(chars) - 1, level))
        row += chars[level]
    print(f"  {y_r[i]:+5.1f} |{row}|")
print(f"        {''.join(['-'] * len(x_r))}")
print(f"       {x_r[0]:+.0f}{' ' * (len(x_r) - 7)}{x_r[-1]:+.0f}")
print(f"                    Weight 1 -->\
")

# Gradient descent on this landscape
x_pos, y_pos = 3.0, 3.0
lr = 0.1
path = [(x_pos, y_pos, loss_fn(x_pos, y_pos))]

for _ in range(30):
    eps = 1e-4
    gx = (loss_fn(x_pos+eps, y_pos) - loss_fn(x_pos-eps, y_pos)) / (2*eps)
    gy = (loss_fn(x_pos, y_pos+eps) - loss_fn(x_pos, y_pos-eps)) / (2*eps)
    x_pos -= lr * gx
    y_pos -= lr * gy
    path.append((x_pos, y_pos, loss_fn(x_pos, y_pos)))

print("=== Gradient Descent Path ===")
print(f"Starting from ({path[0][0]:.1f}, {path[0][1]:.1f}), loss = {path[0][2]:.3f}\
")
print(f"{'Step':>4}  {'Position (w1, w2)':>18}  {'Loss':>7}  {'Change':>8}")
print("-" * 45)
for i in [0, 1, 2, 5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30]:
    change = path[i][2] - path[max(0,i-1)][2] if i > 0 else 0
    print(f"  {i:2d}   ({path[i][0]:+6.3f}, {path[i][1]:+6.3f})   {path[i][2]:7.3f}  {change:+8.4f}")

print(f"\
Total improvement: {path[0][2] - path[-1][2]:.3f}")
print(f"The optimizer found a valley by following the gradient downhill.")

Practical Considerations

Common Pitfalls in Loss Computation

Pitfall 1: Numerical Overflow in Softmax

Without the max-subtraction trick, exp(1000) = ∞ in floating point. Always subtract the maximum logit before exponentiating. This is mathematically equivalent but numerically safe.

Pitfall 2: Log of Zero

If any softmax probability underflows to exactly 0, then log(0) = −∞. Either add a tiny epsilon (log(probs + 1e-10)) or, better yet, use the log-softmax formulation directly, which avoids this entirely.

Pitfall 3: Ignoring Padding Tokens

When sequences have different lengths and are padded, you must not include padding positions in the loss. Use a loss mask that zeroes out padding contributions. Otherwise, the model wastes capacity learning to predict meaningless padding symbols.

What Loss Values to Expect

  • At initialization (random weights): Loss ≈ log(vocab_size). For vocab=50,257: ~10.8
  • After a few steps: Rapidly drops to 7-8 as the model learns token frequencies
  • After significant training: 3-4 for GPT-2 scale on web text
  • Fully converged GPT-2: Loss ~3.0-3.5 (perplexity 20-33)
  • Large models (175B+): Loss ~2.5-3.0 (perplexity 12-20)
Sanity Check: If your initial loss differs significantly from log(vocab_size), something is wrong with your model initialization or loss computation. This is the very first check every practitioner performs when starting a training run.

Summary: The Evaluation Toolkit

In this lecture, we built the complete evaluation toolkit for language model pretraining:

  1. Cross-entropy loss measures the negative log-probability of the correct next token, averaged over all positions. It is the loss function we minimize during training.
  2. Perplexity = exp(loss) — the effective number of tokens the model "chooses between." A perplexity of 20 means the model narrows down the next token to about 20 plausible candidates.
  3. Training vs. validation loss reveals overfitting when the generalization gap starts growing.
  4. The loss landscape provides geometric intuition about what the optimizer navigates and why larger models tend to be easier to train.

With these metrics in hand, we are ready to build the actual training loop. In the next lecture, we will construct the DataLoader that feeds text to the model and implement the complete pretraining loop.

Self-Test: Key Takeaway

Can you explain cross-entropy and perplexity in your own words? If a researcher says "we achieved 15.2 perplexity on WikiText-103," what exactly does that number tell you about the model? How would you use validation perplexity during training to decide when to change your strategy? Why are these two metrics considered the "language of pretraining"?

LECTURE 25 Etapa 5: Preantrenament

Lecția 25: Evaluarea modelelor generative de text

Cross-Entropy Loss, Perplexitate și Măsurarea calității predicțiilor lingvistice ale unui model
45 min de citit Avansat Cuantificarea calității modelului înainte, în timpul și după preantrenament

Introducere: De ce avem nevoie de metrici pentru modelele de limbaj

Am construit acum fiecare componentă a unui Transformer în stil GPT — token embeddings, codificări poziționale, multi-head causal self-attention, rețele feed-forward cu activare GELU, layer normalization, conexiuni reziduale și blocuri Transformer complete stivuite într-un model complet. Dar înainte de a putea antrena acest model, trebuie să răspundem la o întrebare fundamentală: cum știm dacă modelul se îmbunătățește?

Spre deosebire de sarcinile de clasificare unde acuratețea oferă un răspuns clar („ai clasificat corect 92% din etichete"), modelele generative de limbaj pun o provocare mai subtilă. Modelul produce o distribuție de probabilitate peste întregul vocabular la fiecare poziție dintr-o secvență. Nu alege doar un singur cuvânt — atribuie probabilități tuturor token-urilor posibile următoare. Avem nevoie de metrici care surprind cât de bune sunt aceste distribuții de probabilitate.

Ideea centrală: Un model de limbaj perfect ar atribui probabilitatea 1.0 oricărui token care urmează efectiv, și 0.0 fiecărui alt token. Un model teribil ar distribui probabilitatea uniform pe vocabular, ghicind în esență aleator. Metricile noastre măsoară unde se situează un model pe acest spectru.

În această lecție, construim două metrici fundamentale de la zero: cross-entropy loss (funcția pe care o minimizăm în timpul antrenamentului) și perplexitatea (metrica intuitivă de evaluare derivată din aceasta). Acestea nu sunt simple formule abstracte — sunt busola care ghidează fiecare decizie despre rata de învățare, dimensiunea lotului, dimensiunea modelului și durata antrenamentului în timpul preantrenamentului.

De la probabilități la pierdere: Povestea Cross-Entropy

Ce produce de fapt modelul

Amintiți-vă că modelul nostru GPT se termină cu o proiecție liniară de la dimensiunea ascunsă (d_model) la dimensiunea vocabularului (vocab_size). Pentru un vocabular de 50.257 de token-uri (GPT-2), fiecare poziție produce un vector de 50.257 de numere numit logits. Acestea sunt scoruri brute, nenormalizate — orice număr real, pozitiv sau negativ.

Pentru a converti logits-urile în probabilități, aplicăm funcția softmax:

Funcția Softmax

P(token = i) = exp(zi) / ∑j=1V exp(zj)

Aceasta garantează că toate probabilitățile sunt pozitive și însumează 1. Logits-urile mai mari corespund probabilităților mai mari. Softmax-ul este „soft" deoarece atribuie o anumită probabilitate fiecărui token, distribuția devenind mai concentrată pe măsură ce diferențele dintre logits cresc.

Funcția de pierdere Cross-Entropy

Să presupunem că modelul prezice probabilitatea P(token = i) pentru fiecare token, iar token-ul următor real este token-ul t. Pierderea cross-entropy măsoară cât de surprins a fost modelul de token-ul corect:

Pierderea Cross-Entropy (un singur token)

L = −log P(token = t)

Aceasta este pur și simplu log-probabilitatea negativă a răspunsului corect.

De ce această formulă are sens intuitiv:

  • Probabilitate 1.0 pentru token-ul corect: L = −log(1.0) = 0. Predicție perfectă, pierdere zero.
  • Probabilitate 0.5: L = −log(0.5) ≈ 0.693. Decentă dar incertă.
  • Probabilitate 0.01: L = −log(0.01) ≈ 4.605. Foarte surprins de token-ul corect.
  • Probabilitate aproape de 0: L → ∞. Catastrofal de greșit.
Analogie: Meteorologul

Imaginați-vă un meteorolog care atribuie probabilități vremii de mâine. Dacă spune „90% șanse de ploaie" și plouă, pierderea sa este mică (−log(0.9) ≈ 0.105). Dacă spune „5% șanse de ploaie" și plouă, pierderea sa este foarte mare (−log(0.05) ≈ 3.0). Cross-entropy penalizează predicțiile greșite cu încredere mare mult mai sever decât pe cele incerte. Exact asta dorim: un model care spune „sunt 99% sigur că următorul cuvânt este «pisică»" și se dovedește a greși ar trebui să primească o penalizare uriașă.

Trucul LogSoftmax pentru stabilitate numerică

În practică, nu calculăm niciodată explicit probabilitățile softmax și apoi luăm logaritmul. În schimb, folosim identitatea log-softmax, care este mai stabilă numeric:

Log-Softmax (Stabil numeric)

log P(token = i) = (zi − zmax) − log(∑j=1V exp(zj − zmax))

Prin scăderea logitului maxim înainte de exponențiere, evităm calcularea exp pentru numere foarte mari (care ar depăși spre infinit). Scăderea se anulează matematic dar previne catastrofa numerică.

Pentru o secvență completă de T token-uri, calculăm pierderea la fiecare poziție și facem media. Fiecare termen măsoară cât de bine a prezis modelul token-ul de la poziția i dat fiind toate token-urile precedente:

Lseq = −(1/T) ∑i=1T log P(tokeni | token1, ..., tokeni−1)

Python 

import numpy as np
np.random.seed(42)

# ============================================================
# Cross-Entropy Loss from Scratch
# ============================================================

def softmax(logits):
 """Compute softmax probabilities (numerically stable)."""
 shifted = logits - np.max(logits, axis=-1, keepdims=True)
 exp_vals = np.exp(shifted)
 return exp_vals / np.sum(exp_vals, axis=-1, keepdims=True)

def cross_entropy_loss(logits, targets):
 """
 Compute cross-entropy loss from logits and integer targets.

 logits: (batch_size, seq_len, vocab_size) - raw model outputs
 targets: (batch_size, seq_len) - correct next token IDs
 Returns: scalar average loss
 """
 batch_size, seq_len, vocab_size = logits.shape

 # Log-softmax (numerically stable)
 shifted = logits - np.max(logits, axis=-1, keepdims=True)
 log_sum_exp = np.log(np.sum(np.exp(shifted), axis=-1))
 log_probs = shifted - log_sum_exp[..., np.newaxis]

 # Extract log-probability of the correct token at each position
 batch_idx = np.arange(batch_size)[:, np.newaxis]
 seq_idx = np.arange(seq_len)[np.newaxis, :]
 target_log_probs = log_probs[batch_idx, seq_idx, targets]

 return -np.mean(target_log_probs)

# --- Demo: Three scenarios ---
vocab_size, seq_len, batch_size = 10, 5, 2
logits = np.random.randn(batch_size, seq_len, vocab_size)
targets = np.random.randint(0, vocab_size, (batch_size, seq_len))

loss = cross_entropy_loss(logits, targets)
print("=== Cross-Entropy Loss Demo ===")
print(f"Vocabulary size: {vocab_size} | Sequence length: {seq_len}")
print(f"Random model loss: {loss:.4f}")
print(f"Expected for random guessing: -log(1/{vocab_size}) = {-np.log(1/vocab_size):.4f}")
print()

# Near-perfect model: high logit for correct token
perfect = np.full((batch_size, seq_len, vocab_size), -10.0)
for b in range(batch_size):
 for t in range(seq_len):
 perfect[b, t, targets[b, t]] = 10.0
print(f"Near-perfect model loss: {cross_entropy_loss(perfect, targets):.6f}")
print(" (Close to 0: the model is confident about the right answers)")

# Deliberately wrong model: high logit for wrong tokens
wrong = np.full((batch_size, seq_len, vocab_size), 10.0)
for b in range(batch_size):
 for t in range(seq_len):
 wrong[b, t, targets[b, t]] = -10.0
print(f"Deliberately wrong loss: {cross_entropy_loss(wrong, targets):.4f}")
print(" (Very high: the model is confident about wrong answers)")

Perplexitatea: Făcând pierderea intuitivă

Pierderea cross-entropy este numărul pe care îl optimizăm, dar este greu de interpretat direct. Ce înseamnă de fapt o pierdere de 3.2? Este bună sau rea? Aici intervine perplexitatea — transformă valoarea abstractă a pierderii în ceva ce puteți înțelege intuitiv.

Perplexitatea

PPL = exp(L)

unde L este pierderea medie cross-entropy per token. Perplexitatea reprezintă numărul efectiv de token-uri dintre care modelul alege la fiecare pas. Dacă un model are perplexitate 100, înseamnă că modelul este, în medie, la fel de incert ca și cum ar alege uniform dintre 100 de token-uri la fel de probabile.

O perplexitate mai mică înseamnă întotdeauna un model mai bun. Iată puncte de referință:

  • PPL = 1: Predicție perfectă. Modelul știe întotdeauna exact ce urmează.
  • PPL = vocab_size (de ex., 50.257): Ghicire aleatorie. Modelul nu a învățat nimic.
  • GPT-2 Small: PPL ~35 pe WikiText-103 — restrângere la ~35 de token-uri plauzibile următoare.
  • GPT-3 (175B): PPL ~20 pe benchmark-uri similare.
  • Cele mai performante modele (2024-2025): Perplexități în jurul valorii de zece.
Analogie: Testul cu variante multiple

Imaginați-vă că susțineți un test în care fiecare întrebare are V variante de răspuns. Perplexitatea vă spune numărul efectiv de variante pe care modelul le consideră plauzibile. O perplexitate de 5 înseamnă că modelul a restrâns opțiunile la aproximativ 5 variante plauzibile, chiar dacă V este 50.000. O perplexitate de 50.000 înseamnă că toate token-urile par la fel de probabile — modelul nu a învățat nimic despre structura limbajului.

De ce perplexitatea este ideală pentru compararea modelelor

Perplexitatea are mai multe proprietăți care o fac metrica standard de evaluare:

  1. Invariantă la scală: O PPL de 20 înseamnă același lucru indiferent de dimensiunea vocabularului sau a setului de date.
  2. Multiplicativă: Înjumătățirea perplexității (de ex., de la 40 la 20) înseamnă că modelul și-a dublat precizia predictivă.
  3. Comparabilă: Puteți compara direct PPL între arhitecturi (același vocabular și set de evaluare).
  4. Mai mic e mai bine: Interpretare simplă și lipsită de ambiguitate.
Python 

import numpy as np
np.random.seed(42)

# ============================================================
# Perplexity: From Loss to Intuition
# ============================================================

def compute_perplexity(logits, targets):
 """Compute both cross-entropy loss and perplexity."""
 batch_size, seq_len, vocab_size = logits.shape
 shifted = logits - np.max(logits, axis=-1, keepdims=True)
 log_sum_exp = np.log(np.sum(np.exp(shifted), axis=-1))
 log_probs = shifted - log_sum_exp[..., np.newaxis]
 batch_idx = np.arange(batch_size)[:, np.newaxis]
 seq_idx = np.arange(seq_len)[np.newaxis, :]
 target_log_probs = log_probs[batch_idx, seq_idx, targets]
 avg_loss = -np.mean(target_log_probs)
 return avg_loss, np.exp(avg_loss)

# Simulate models at different quality levels
vocab_size, seq_len, batch_size = 1000, 50, 4
targets = np.random.randint(0, vocab_size, (batch_size, seq_len))

print("=== Perplexity at Different Model Quality Levels ===")
print(f"Vocabulary size: {vocab_size}")
print()
print(f"{'Model Quality':<22} {'Loss':>7} {'Perplexity':>11} {'Interpretation'}")
print("-" * 75)

configs = [

]
for name, noise_scale, boost in configs:

print()
print("Key insight: As the model improves, perplexity drops from ~1000")
print("(random guessing across 1000 tokens) toward single digits.")
print("Each improvement means the model is more 'certain' about what comes next.")

Pierderea pe setul de antrenament vs. validare: Detectarea supraantrenării

În practică, nu ne uităm niciodată doar la un singur număr de pierdere. Calculăm pierderea pe două seturi de date separate:

  • Pierderea pe antrenament: Calculată pe datele pe care modelul le-a văzut și din care a învățat. Aceasta ar trebui să scadă întotdeauna.
  • Pierderea pe validare: Calculată pe date pe care modelul nu le-a văzut niciodată. Aceasta relevă dacă modelul învață tipare generale sau doar memorează datele de antrenament.

Semnalul de supraantrenare

Relația dintre pierderea pe antrenament și pe validare relevă trei regimuri de antrenament:

  • Subantrenare: Ambele pierderi sunt mari. Modelul nu a învățat suficient. Continuați antrenamentul.
  • Ajustare bună: Ambele pierderi sunt mici și aproape egale. Modelul a învățat tipare generalizabile.
  • Supraantrenare: Pierderea pe antrenament continuă să scadă, dar pierderea pe validare începe să crească. Modelul memorează.

Diferența dintre pierderea pe validare și cea pe antrenament se numește decalajul de generalizare. Un decalaj în creștere este cel mai clar semnal că supraantrenarea a început.

Metrici la nivel de token vs. la nivel de secvență

Există o distincție importantă care merită înțeleasă:

  • Metrici la nivel de token (pierdere, perplexitate per token): Folosite în timpul preantrenamentului. Oferă un semnal neted și diferențiabil pentru optimizator.
  • Metrici la nivel de secvență (BLEU, ROUGE, evaluare umană): Evaluează secvențele generate complet. Rezervate pentru evaluarea sarcinilor din aval după preantrenament.

np.random.seed(42)

Peisajul pierderii: Vizualizarea a ceea ce vede optimizatorul

Când antrenăm un model, optimizatorul navighează un peisaj al pierderii de dimensionalitate înaltă — o suprafață unde fiecare punct corespunde unui anumit set de ponderi ale modelului, iar înălțimea este valoarea pierderii. Înțelegerea caracteristicilor cheie ale acestui peisaj construiește o intuiție crucială:

  • Minimul global: Cel mai jos punct absolut. Găsirea acestuia este în general imposibilă pentru rețelele neurale.
  • Minime locale: Puncte mai joase decât vecinii lor imediați. Pentru modelele mari, acestea sunt adesea „suficient de bune" — cercetările arată că tind să aibă valori similare ale pierderii.
  • Puncte de șa: Minime în unele direcții, maxime în altele. Mai comune decât minimele locale în dimensiuni înalte și pot încetini semnificativ antrenamentul.
  • Regiuni plate (platouri): Zone mari unde pierderea abia se schimbă. Gradienții sunt aproape de zero, făcând progresul dureros de lent.

Cercetările au arătat că modelele mai mari tind să aibă peisaje mai netede, mai bine comportate, cu mai puține minime locale problematice. Acesta este unul dintre motivele pentru care creșterea dimensiunii modelului face adesea antrenamentul mai ușor, nu mai greu — o constatare contraintuitivă dar bine documentată.

Considerații practice

Capcane frecvente în calculul pierderii

Capcana 1: Depășire numerică în Softmax

Fără trucul scăderii maximului, exp(1000) = ∞ în virgulă mobilă. Scădeți întotdeauna logitul maxim înainte de exponențiere. Aceasta este echivalentă matematic dar sigură numeric.

Capcana 2: Logaritmul din zero

Dacă vreo probabilitate softmax scade la exact 0, atunci log(0) = −∞. Fie adăugați un epsilon minuscul (log(probs + 1e-10)), fie, și mai bine, folosiți formularea log-softmax direct, care evită complet această problemă.

Capcana 3: Ignorarea token-urilor de padding

Când secvențele au lungimi diferite și sunt completate cu padding, nu trebuie să includeți pozițiile de padding în pierdere. Folosiți o mască de pierdere care anulează contribuțiile padding-ului. Altfel, modelul irosește capacitate învățând să prezică simboluri de padding lipsite de sens.

Ce valori ale pierderii să așteptați

  • La inițializare (ponderi aleatorii): Pierdere ≈ log(vocab_size). Pentru vocab=50.257: ~10.8
  • După câțiva pași: Scade rapid la 7-8 pe măsură ce modelul învață frecvențele token-urilor
  • După antrenament semnificativ: 3-4 pentru scala GPT-2 pe text de pe web
  • GPT-2 complet convergent: Pierdere ~3.0-3.5 (perplexitate 20-33)
  • Modele mari (175B+): Pierdere ~2.5-3.0 (perplexitate 12-20)
Verificare de bun simț: Dacă pierderea inițială diferă semnificativ de log(vocab_size), ceva este greșit cu inițializarea modelului sau cu calculul pierderii. Aceasta este prima verificare pe care o face fiecare practician la începutul unei rulări de antrenament.

Rezumat: Setul de instrumente de evaluare

În această lecție, am construit setul complet de instrumente de evaluare pentru preantrenamentul modelelor de limbaj:

  1. Pierderea cross-entropy măsoară log-probabilitatea negativă a token-ului următor corect, mediată pe toate pozițiile. Este funcția de pierdere pe care o minimizăm în timpul antrenamentului.
  2. Perplexitatea = exp(pierdere) — numărul efectiv de token-uri dintre care modelul „alege". O perplexitate de 20 înseamnă că modelul restrânge token-ul următor la aproximativ 20 de candidați plauzibili.
  3. Pierderea pe antrenament vs. validare relevă supraantrenarea când decalajul de generalizare începe să crească.
  4. Peisajul pierderii oferă intuiție geometrică despre ce navighează optimizatorul și de ce modelele mai mari tind să fie mai ușor de antrenat.

Cu aceste metrici la îndemână, suntem pregătiți să construim bucla de antrenament propriu-zisă. În lecția următoare, vom construi DataLoader-ul care alimentează modelul cu text și vom implementa bucla completă de preantrenament.

Concluzia cheie

Cross-entropy și perplexitatea sunt limbajul preantrenamentului. Când cercetătorii spun „am obținut perplexitate 15.2 pe WikiText-103", ei vă spun exact cât de bine prezice modelul lor limbajul. Când monitorizați antrenamentul și vedeți perplexitatea pe validare stagnând, știți că este momentul să vă ajustați strategia. Stăpâniți aceste metrici, și veți ști întotdeauna unde se situează modelul dumneavoastră.

Διάλεξη 25: Αξιολόγηση γεννητικών μοντέλων κειμένου

Cross-Entropy Loss, Perplexity και Μέτρηση του πόσο καλά ένα μοντέλο προβλέπει τη γλώσσα
45 λεπτά ανάγνωση Προχωρημένο Ποσοτικοποίηση της ποιότητας του μοντέλου πριν, κατά τη διάρκεια και μετά την προεκπαίδευση

Εισαγωγή: Γιατί χρειαζόμαστε μετρικές για τα γλωσσικά μοντέλα

Έχουμε πλέον κατασκευάσει κάθε συστατικό ενός Transformer τύπου GPT — token embeddings, positional encodings, multi-head causal self-attention, δίκτυα feed-forward με ενεργοποίηση GELU, layer normalization, residual connections και πλήρη Transformer blocks στοιβαγμένα σε ένα ολοκληρωμένο μοντέλο. Αλλά πριν μπορέσουμε να εκπαιδεύσουμε αυτό το μοντέλο, πρέπει να απαντήσουμε σε ένα θεμελιώδες ερώτημα: πώς ξέρουμε αν το μοντέλο βελτιώνεται;

Σε αντίθεση με τα tasks ταξινόμησης όπου η ακρίβεια δίνει μια σαφή απάντηση («ταξινομήσατε σωστά το 92% των ετικετών»), τα γεννητικά γλωσσικά μοντέλα θέτουν μια πιο λεπτή πρόκληση. Το μοντέλο παράγει μια κατανομή πιθανοτήτων σε ολόκληρο το λεξιλόγιο σε κάθε θέση μιας ακολουθίας. Δεν επιλέγει απλά μία λέξη — εκχωρεί πιθανότητες σε όλα τα πιθανά επόμενα tokens. Χρειαζόμαστε μετρικές που αποτυπώνουν πόσο καλές είναι αυτές οι κατανομές πιθανοτήτων.

Η κεντρική ιδέα: Ένα τέλειο γλωσσικό μοντέλο θα εκχωρούσε πιθανότητα 1.0 σε όποιο token πραγματικά ακολουθεί, και 0.0 σε κάθε άλλο token. Ένα τρομερό μοντέλο θα κατανείμε την πιθανότητα ομοιόμορφα σε ολόκληρο το λεξιλόγιο, μαντεύοντας ουσιαστικά τυχαία. Οι μετρικές μας μετρούν πού βρίσκεται ένα μοντέλο σε αυτό το φάσμα.

Σε αυτή τη διάλεξη, κατασκευάζουμε δύο θεμελιώδεις μετρικές από το μηδέν: cross-entropy loss (η συνάρτηση που ελαχιστοποιούμε κατά την εκπαίδευση) και perplexity (η διαισθητική μετρική αξιολόγησης που προκύπτει από αυτήν). Αυτές δεν είναι απλώς αφηρημένοι τύποι — είναι η πυξίδα που καθοδηγεί κάθε απόφαση σχετικά με το ρυθμό μάθησης, το μέγεθος παρτίδας, το μέγεθος μοντέλου και τη διάρκεια εκπαίδευσης κατά την προεκπαίδευση.

Από τις πιθανότητες στην απώλεια: Η ιστορία του Cross-Entropy

Τι παράγει πραγματικά το μοντέλο

Θυμηθείτε ότι το μοντέλο GPT μας τελειώνει με μια γραμμική προβολή από την κρυφή διάσταση (d_model) στο μέγεθος λεξιλογίου (vocab_size). Για ένα λεξιλόγιο 50.257 tokens (GPT-2), κάθε θέση παράγει ένα διάνυσμα 50.257 αριθμών που ονομάζονται logits. Αυτά είναι ακατέργαστες, μη κανονικοποιημένες βαθμολογίες — οποιοσδήποτε πραγματικός αριθμός, θετικός ή αρνητικός.

Για να μετατρέψουμε τα logits σε πιθανότητες, εφαρμόζουμε τη συνάρτηση softmax:

Συνάρτηση Softmax

P(token = i) = exp(zi) / ∑j=1V exp(zj)

Αυτό εγγυάται ότι όλες οι πιθανότητες είναι θετικές και αθροίζουν στο 1. Μεγαλύτερα logits αντιστοιχούν σε μεγαλύτερες πιθανότητες. Η softmax είναι «ομαλή» επειδή δίνει κάποια πιθανότητα σε κάθε token, με την κατανομή να γίνεται πιο αιχμηρή καθώς αυξάνονται οι διαφορές logits.

Η συνάρτηση απώλειας Cross-Entropy

Ας υποθέσουμε ότι το μοντέλο προβλέπει πιθανότητα P(token = i) για κάθε token, και το πραγματικό επόμενο token είναι το token t. Η απώλεια cross-entropy μετρά πόσο εκπλαγμένο ήταν το μοντέλο από το σωστό token:

Απώλεια Cross-Entropy (μεμονωμένο token)

L = −log P(token = t)

Αυτό είναι απλά η αρνητική λογ-πιθανότητα της σωστής απάντησης.

Γιατί αυτός ο τύπος έχει διαισθητικό νόημα:

  • Πιθανότητα 1.0 για το σωστό token: L = −log(1.0) = 0. Τέλεια πρόβλεψη, μηδενική απώλεια.
  • Πιθανότητα 0.5: L = −log(0.5) ≈ 0.693. Αξιοπρεπής αλλά αβέβαιη.
  • Πιθανότητα 0.01: L = −log(0.01) ≈ 4.605. Πολύ εκπλαγμένο από το σωστό token.
  • Πιθανότητα κοντά στο 0: L → ∞. Καταστροφικά λάθος.
Αναλογία: Ο μετεωρολόγος

Φανταστείτε έναν μετεωρολόγο που εκχωρεί πιθανότητες στον αυριανό καιρό. Αν πει «90% πιθανότητα βροχής» και βρέξει, η απώλειά του είναι χαμηλή (−log(0.9) ≈ 0.105). Αν πει «5% πιθανότητα βροχής» και βρέξει, η απώλειά του είναι πολύ υψηλή (−log(0.05) ≈ 3.0). Η cross-entropy τιμωρεί τις σίγουρες λανθασμένες προβλέψεις πολύ πιο αυστηρά από τις αβέβαιες. Αυτό ακριβώς θέλουμε: ένα μοντέλο που λέει «είμαι 99% σίγουρο ότι η επόμενη λέξη είναι "γάτα"» και αποδεικνύεται λάθος θα πρέπει να λάβει τεράστια ποινή.

Το τέχνασμα LogSoftmax για αριθμητική σταθερότητα

Στην πράξη, δεν υπολογίζουμε ποτέ ρητά τις πιθανότητες softmax και μετά παίρνουμε τον λογάριθμο. Αντ' αυτού, χρησιμοποιούμε την ταυτότητα log-softmax, η οποία είναι πιο αριθμητικά σταθερή:

Log-Softmax (Αριθμητικά σταθερή)

log P(token = i) = (zi − zmax) − log(∑j=1V exp(zj − zmax))

Αφαιρώντας το μέγιστο logit πριν από την εκθετικοποίηση, αποφεύγουμε τον υπολογισμό του exp πολύ μεγάλων αριθμών (που θα υπερχειλίσουν στο άπειρο). Η αφαίρεση αλληλοαναιρείται μαθηματικά αλλά αποτρέπει αριθμητική καταστροφή.

Για μια πλήρη ακολουθία T tokens, υπολογίζουμε την απώλεια σε κάθε θέση και παίρνουμε τον μέσο όρο. Κάθε όρος μετρά πόσο καλά πρόβλεψε το μοντέλο το token στη θέση i δεδομένων όλων των προηγούμενων tokens:

Lseq = −(1/T) ∑i=1T log P(tokeni | token1, ..., tokeni−1)

Python 

import numpy as np
np.random.seed(42)

# ============================================================
# Cross-Entropy Loss from Scratch
# ============================================================

def softmax(logits):
 """Compute softmax probabilities (numerically stable)."""
 shifted = logits - np.max(logits, axis=-1, keepdims=True)
 exp_vals = np.exp(shifted)
 return exp_vals / np.sum(exp_vals, axis=-1, keepdims=True)

def cross_entropy_loss(logits, targets):
 """
 Compute cross-entropy loss from logits and integer targets.

 logits: (batch_size, seq_len, vocab_size) - raw model outputs
 targets: (batch_size, seq_len) - correct next token IDs
 Returns: scalar average loss
 """
 batch_size, seq_len, vocab_size = logits.shape

 # Log-softmax (numerically stable)
 shifted = logits - np.max(logits, axis=-1, keepdims=True)
 log_sum_exp = np.log(np.sum(np.exp(shifted), axis=-1))
 log_probs = shifted - log_sum_exp[..., np.newaxis]

 # Extract log-probability of the correct token at each position
 batch_idx = np.arange(batch_size)[:, np.newaxis]
 seq_idx = np.arange(seq_len)[np.newaxis, :]
 target_log_probs = log_probs[batch_idx, seq_idx, targets]

 return -np.mean(target_log_probs)

# --- Demo: Three scenarios ---
vocab_size, seq_len, batch_size = 10, 5, 2
logits = np.random.randn(batch_size, seq_len, vocab_size)
targets = np.random.randint(0, vocab_size, (batch_size, seq_len))

loss = cross_entropy_loss(logits, targets)
print("=== Cross-Entropy Loss Demo ===")
print(f"Vocabulary size: {vocab_size} | Sequence length: {seq_len}")
print(f"Random model loss: {loss:.4f}")
print(f"Expected for random guessing: -log(1/{vocab_size}) = {-np.log(1/vocab_size):.4f}")
print()

# Near-perfect model: high logit for correct token
perfect = np.full((batch_size, seq_len, vocab_size), -10.0)
for b in range(batch_size):
 for t in range(seq_len):
 perfect[b, t, targets[b, t]] = 10.0
print(f"Near-perfect model loss: {cross_entropy_loss(perfect, targets):.6f}")
print(" (Close to 0: the model is confident about the right answers)")

# Deliberately wrong model: high logit for wrong tokens
wrong = np.full((batch_size, seq_len, vocab_size), 10.0)
for b in range(batch_size):
 for t in range(seq_len):
 wrong[b, t, targets[b, t]] = -10.0
print(f"Deliberately wrong loss: {cross_entropy_loss(wrong, targets):.4f}")
print(" (Very high: the model is confident about wrong answers)")

Perplexity: Κάνοντας την απώλεια διαισθητική

Η απώλεια cross-entropy είναι ο αριθμός που βελτιστοποιούμε, αλλά είναι δύσκολο να ερμηνευτεί άμεσα. Τι σημαίνει πραγματικά μια απώλεια 3.2; Είναι καλό ή κακό; Εδώ μπαίνει η perplexity — μετατρέπει την αφηρημένη τιμή απώλειας σε κάτι που μπορείτε να κατανοήσετε διαισθητικά.

Perplexity

PPL = exp(L)

όπου L είναι η μέση απώλεια cross-entropy ανά token. Η perplexity αναπαριστά τον πραγματικό αριθμό tokens ανάμεσα στα οποία επιλέγει το μοντέλο σε κάθε βήμα. Αν ένα μοντέλο έχει perplexity 100, σημαίνει ότι το μοντέλο είναι, κατά μέσο όρο, τόσο αβέβαιο σαν να επέλεγε ομοιόμορφα ανάμεσα σε 100 εξίσου πιθανά tokens.

Χαμηλότερη perplexity σημαίνει πάντα καλύτερο μοντέλο. Ακολουθούν σημεία αναφοράς:

  • PPL = 1: Τέλεια πρόβλεψη. Το μοντέλο ξέρει πάντα ακριβώς τι ακολουθεί.
  • PPL = vocab_size (π.χ., 50.257): Τυχαία εικασία. Το μοντέλο δεν έχει μάθει τίποτα.
  • GPT-2 Small: PPL ~35 στο WikiText-103 — περιορισμός σε ~35 πιθανά επόμενα tokens.
  • GPT-3 (175B): PPL ~20 σε παρόμοια benchmarks.
  • Τελευταία λέξη τεχνολογίας (2024-2025): Perplexity στα χαμηλά δεκαδικά.
Αναλογία: Το τεστ πολλαπλής επιλογής

Φανταστείτε ότι δίνετε ένα τεστ όπου κάθε ερώτηση έχει V επιλογές απάντησης. Η perplexity σας λέει τον πραγματικό αριθμό επιλογών που το μοντέλο θεωρεί πιθανές. Μια perplexity 5 σημαίνει ότι το μοντέλο έχει περιορίσει τις επιλογές σε περίπου 5 πιθανές, ακόμα κι αν V είναι 50.000. Μια perplexity 50.000 σημαίνει ότι όλα τα tokens φαίνονται εξίσου πιθανά — το μοντέλο δεν έχει μάθει τίποτα για τη δομή της γλώσσας.

Γιατί η Perplexity είναι ιδανική για σύγκριση μοντέλων

Η perplexity έχει αρκετές ιδιότητες που τη καθιστούν την τυπική μετρική αξιολόγησης:

  1. Αμετάβλητη ως προς την κλίμακα: PPL 20 σημαίνει το ίδιο πράγμα ανεξάρτητα από το μέγεθος λεξιλογίου ή συνόλου δεδομένων.
  2. Πολλαπλασιαστική: Ο υποδιπλασιασμός της perplexity (π.χ., από 40 σε 20) σημαίνει ότι το μοντέλο διπλασίασε την προβλεπτική του ακρίβεια.
  3. Συγκρίσιμη: Μπορείτε να συγκρίνετε απευθείας PPL μεταξύ αρχιτεκτονικών (ίδιο λεξιλόγιο και σύνολο αξιολόγησης).
  4. Χαμηλότερο σημαίνει καλύτερο: Απλή, αδιαμφισβήτητη ερμηνεία.

import numpy as np
np.random.seed(42)

# ============================================================
# Perplexity: From Loss to Intuition
# ============================================================

def compute_perplexity(logits, targets):
 """Compute both cross-entropy loss and perplexity."""
 batch_size, seq_len, vocab_size = logits.shape
 shifted = logits - np.max(logits, axis=-1, keepdims=True)
 log_sum_exp = np.log(np.sum(np.exp(shifted), axis=-1))
 log_probs = shifted - log_sum_exp[..., np.newaxis]
 batch_idx = np.arange(batch_size)[:, np.newaxis]
 seq_idx = np.arange(seq_len)[np.newaxis, :]
 target_log_probs = log_probs[batch_idx, seq_idx, targets]
 avg_loss = -np.mean(target_log_probs)
 return avg_loss, np.exp(avg_loss)

# Simulate models at different quality levels
vocab_size, seq_len, batch_size = 1000, 50, 4
targets = np.random.randint(0, vocab_size, (batch_size, seq_len))

print("=== Perplexity at Different Model Quality Levels ===")
print(f"Vocabulary size: {vocab_size}")
print()
print(f"{'Model Quality':<22} {'Loss':>7} {'Perplexity':>11} {'Interpretation'}")
print("-" * 75)

configs = [
 ("Random (untrained)", 0.01, 0.0),
 ("Slightly trained", 0.5, 2.0),
 ("Moderately trained", 0.3, 4.0),
 ("Well-trained", 0.2, 6.0),
 ("Excellent", 0.1, 10.0),
]
for name, noise_scale, boost in configs:
 logits = np.random.randn(batch_size, seq_len, vocab_size) * noise_scale
 if boost > 0:
 for b in range(batch_size):
 for t in range(seq_len):
 logits[b, t, targets[b, t]] += boost
 loss, ppl = compute_perplexity(logits, targets)
 print(f" {name:<20} {loss:>7.3f} {ppl:>11.1f} Choosing among ~{ppl:.0f} tokens")

print()
print("Key insight: As the model improves, perplexity drops from ~1000")
print("(random guessing across 1000 tokens) toward single digits.")
print("Each improvement means the model is more 'certain' about what comes next.")

Απώλεια εκπαίδευσης vs. επικύρωσης: Ανίχνευση υπερπροσαρμογής

Στην πράξη, δεν εξετάζουμε ποτέ απλά έναν μεμονωμένο αριθμό απώλειας. Υπολογίζουμε την απώλεια σε δύο ξεχωριστά σύνολα δεδομένων:

  • Απώλεια εκπαίδευσης: Υπολογίζεται στα δεδομένα που το μοντέλο έχει δει και από τα οποία έχει μάθει. Αυτή θα πρέπει πάντα να μειώνεται.
  • Απώλεια επικύρωσης: Υπολογίζεται σε δεδομένα που το μοντέλο δεν έχει δει ποτέ. Αυτή αποκαλύπτει αν το μοντέλο μαθαίνει γενικά πρότυπα ή απλά απομνημονεύει τα δεδομένα εκπαίδευσης.

Το σήμα υπερπροσαρμογής

Η σχέση μεταξύ απώλειας εκπαίδευσης και επικύρωσης αποκαλύπτει τρία καθεστώτα εκπαίδευσης:

  • Υποπροσαρμογή: Και οι δύο απώλειες είναι υψηλές. Το μοντέλο δεν έχει μάθει αρκετά. Συνεχίστε την εκπαίδευση.
  • Καλή προσαρμογή: Και οι δύο απώλειες είναι χαμηλές και κοντά μεταξύ τους. Το μοντέλο έχει μάθει γενικεύσιμα πρότυπα.
  • Υπερπροσαρμογή: Η απώλεια εκπαίδευσης συνεχίζει να μειώνεται αλλά η απώλεια επικύρωσης αρχίζει να αυξάνεται. Το μοντέλο απομνημονεύει.

Η διαφορά μεταξύ της απώλειας επικύρωσης και εκπαίδευσης ονομάζεται κενό γενίκευσης. Ένα αυξανόμενο κενό είναι το πιο σαφές σήμα ότι η υπερπροσαρμογή έχει ξεκινήσει.

Μετρικές σε επίπεδο token vs. σε επίπεδο ακολουθίας

Υπάρχει μια σημαντική διάκριση που αξίζει να κατανοηθεί:

  • Μετρικές σε επίπεδο token (απώλεια, perplexity ανά token): Χρησιμοποιούνται κατά την προεκπαίδευση. Παρέχουν ένα ομαλό, παραγωγίσιμο σήμα στον βελτιστοποιητή.
  • Μετρικές σε επίπεδο ακολουθίας (BLEU, ROUGE, ανθρώπινη αξιολόγηση): Αξιολογούν πλήρεις παραγόμενες ακολουθίες. Προορίζονται για αξιολόγηση downstream tasks μετά την προεκπαίδευση.

print("This divergence is the classic overfitting signature.")

Το τοπίο απώλειας: Οπτικοποιώντας αυτό που βλέπει ο βελτιστοποιητής

Όταν εκπαιδεύουμε ένα μοντέλο, ο βελτιστοποιητής πλοηγείται σε ένα υψηλοδιάστατο τοπίο απώλειας — μια επιφάνεια όπου κάθε σημείο αντιστοιχεί σε ένα συγκεκριμένο σύνολο βαρών του μοντέλου, και το ύψος είναι η τιμή της απώλειας. Η κατανόηση των βασικών χαρακτηριστικών αυτού του τοπίου χτίζει κρίσιμη διαίσθηση:

  • Ολικό ελάχιστο: Το απόλυτα χαμηλότερο σημείο. Η εύρεσή του είναι γενικά αδύνατη για νευρωνικά δίκτυα.
  • Τοπικά ελάχιστα: Σημεία χαμηλότερα από τους άμεσους γείτονές τους. Για μεγάλα μοντέλα, αυτά είναι συχνά «αρκετά καλά» — η έρευνα δείχνει ότι τείνουν να έχουν παρόμοιες τιμές απώλειας.
  • Σαγματικά σημεία: Ελάχιστα σε κάποιες κατευθύνσεις, μέγιστα σε άλλες. Πιο συχνά από τα τοπικά ελάχιστα σε υψηλές διαστάσεις και μπορούν να επιβραδύνουν σημαντικά την εκπαίδευση.
  • Επίπεδες περιοχές (οροπέδια): Μεγάλες περιοχές όπου η απώλεια σχεδόν δεν αλλάζει. Οι κλίσεις είναι κοντά στο μηδέν, κάνοντας την πρόοδο οδυνηρά αργή.

Η έρευνα έχει δείξει ότι τα μεγαλύτερα μοντέλα τείνουν να έχουν ομαλότερα, καλύτερα συμπεριφερόμενα τοπία με λιγότερα προβληματικά τοπικά ελάχιστα. Αυτός είναι ένας λόγος που η αύξηση του μεγέθους μοντέλου συχνά κάνει την εκπαίδευση ευκολότερη, όχι δυσκολότερη — ένα αντιδιαισθητικό αλλά καλά τεκμηριωμένο εύρημα.

Πρακτικές σκέψεις

Συνηθισμένες παγίδες στον υπολογισμό απώλειας

Παγίδα 1: Αριθμητική υπερχείλιση στη Softmax

Χωρίς το τέχνασμα αφαίρεσης του μεγίστου, exp(1000) = ∞ σε κινητής υποδιαστολής. Πάντα αφαιρείτε το μέγιστο logit πριν από την εκθετικοποίηση. Αυτό είναι μαθηματικά ισοδύναμο αλλά αριθμητικά ασφαλές.

Παγίδα 2: Λογάριθμος του μηδενός

Αν κάποια πιθανότητα softmax υποχειλίσει σε ακριβώς 0, τότε log(0) = −∞. Είτε προσθέστε ένα ελάχιστο epsilon (log(probs + 1e-10)), είτε, ακόμα καλύτερα, χρησιμοποιήστε τη μορφή log-softmax απευθείας, που αποφεύγει εντελώς αυτό το πρόβλημα.

Παγίδα 3: Αγνόηση tokens συμπλήρωσης

Όταν οι ακολουθίες έχουν διαφορετικά μήκη και συμπληρώνονται με padding, δεν πρέπει να συμπεριλαμβάνετε τις θέσεις padding στην απώλεια. Χρησιμοποιήστε μια μάσκα απώλειας που μηδενίζει τις συνεισφορές του padding. Διαφορετικά, το μοντέλο σπαταλά χωρητικότητα μαθαίνοντας να προβλέπει χωρίς νόημα σύμβολα padding.

Τι τιμές απώλειας να αναμένετε

  • Κατά την αρχικοποίηση (τυχαία βάρη): Απώλεια ≈ log(vocab_size). Για vocab=50.257: ~10.8
  • Μετά από λίγα βήματα: Πέφτει γρήγορα στο 7-8 καθώς το μοντέλο μαθαίνει τις συχνότητες tokens
  • Μετά από σημαντική εκπαίδευση: 3-4 για κλίμακα GPT-2 σε κείμενο ιστού
  • Πλήρως συγκλίνον GPT-2: Απώλεια ~3.0-3.5 (perplexity 20-33)
  • Μεγάλα μοντέλα (175B+): Απώλεια ~2.5-3.0 (perplexity 12-20)
Έλεγχος λογικής: Αν η αρχική σας απώλεια διαφέρει σημαντικά από log(vocab_size), κάτι δεν πάει καλά με την αρχικοποίηση του μοντέλου ή τον υπολογισμό απώλειας. Αυτός είναι ο πρώτος έλεγχος που κάνει κάθε επαγγελματίας όταν ξεκινά μια εκτέλεση εκπαίδευσης.

Σύνοψη: Η εργαλειοθήκη αξιολόγησης

Σε αυτή τη διάλεξη, κατασκευάσαμε την πλήρη εργαλειοθήκη αξιολόγησης για την προεκπαίδευση γλωσσικών μοντέλων:

  1. Η απώλεια cross-entropy μετρά την αρνητική λογ-πιθανότητα του σωστού επόμενου token, με μέσο όρο σε όλες τις θέσεις. Είναι η συνάρτηση απώλειας που ελαχιστοποιούμε κατά την εκπαίδευση.
  2. Perplexity = exp(απώλεια) — ο πραγματικός αριθμός tokens μεταξύ των οποίων «επιλέγει» το μοντέλο. Μια perplexity 20 σημαίνει ότι το μοντέλο περιορίζει το επόμενο token σε περίπου 20 πιθανούς υποψήφιους.
  3. Απώλεια εκπαίδευσης vs. επικύρωσης αποκαλύπτει υπερπροσαρμογή όταν το κενό γενίκευσης αρχίζει να αυξάνεται.
  4. Το τοπίο απώλειας παρέχει γεωμετρική διαίσθηση για το τι πλοηγεί ο βελτιστοποιητής και γιατί τα μεγαλύτερα μοντέλα τείνουν να εκπαιδεύονται ευκολότερα.

Με αυτές τις μετρικές στα χέρια μας, είμαστε έτοιμοι να κατασκευάσουμε τον πραγματικό βρόχο εκπαίδευσης. Στην επόμενη διάλεξη, θα κατασκευάσουμε τον DataLoader που τροφοδοτεί κείμενο στο μοντέλο και θα υλοποιήσουμε τον πλήρη βρόχο προεκπαίδευσης.

Βασικό συμπέρασμα

Η cross-entropy και η perplexity είναι η γλώσσα της προεκπαίδευσης. Όταν οι ερευνητές λένε «πετύχαμε perplexity 15.2 στο WikiText-103», σας λένε ακριβώς πόσο καλά προβλέπει τη γλώσσα το μοντέλο τους. Όταν παρακολουθείτε την εκπαίδευση και βλέπετε τη perplexity επικύρωσης να σταθεροποιείται, ξέρετε ότι ήρθε η ώρα να προσαρμόσετε τη στρατηγική σας. LEKTION 25 Stufe 5: Pretraining

Bewertung generativer Textmodelle

Cross-Entropy-Loss, Perplexität und wie man misst, wie gut ein Modell Sprache vorhersagt
45 Min. Lesezeit Fortgeschritten Quantifizierung der Modellqualität vor, während und nach dem Pretraining

Einführung: Warum wir Metriken für Sprachmodelle brauchen

Wir haben nun jede Komponente eines GPT-artigen Transformers gebaut — Token-Embeddings, Positional Encodings, Multi-Head Causal Self-Attention, Feed-Forward-Netzwerke mit GELU-Aktivierung, Layer-Normalisierung, Residualverbindungen und vollständige Transformer-Blöcke, gestapelt zu einem kompletten Modell. Doch bevor wir dieses Modell trainieren können, müssen wir eine grundlegende Frage beantworten: Woher wissen wir, dass das Modell besser wird?

Anders als bei Klassifikationsaufgaben, bei denen die Genauigkeit eine klare Antwort liefert ("92 % der Labels waren korrekt"), stellen generative Sprachmodelle eine subtilere Herausforderung dar. Das Modell gibt an jeder Position einer Sequenz eine Wahrscheinlichkeitsverteilung über das gesamte Vokabular aus. Es wählt nicht nur ein einziges Wort — es weist allen möglichen nächsten Token Wahrscheinlichkeiten zu. Wir brauchen Metriken, die erfassen, wie gut diese Wahrscheinlichkeitsverteilungen sind.

Die Kernidee: Ein perfektes Sprachmodell würde dem tatsächlich folgenden Token die Wahrscheinlichkeit 1,0 zuweisen und jedem anderen Token 0,0. Ein schlechtes Modell würde die Wahrscheinlichkeit gleichmäßig über das Vokabular verteilen und im Wesentlichen zufällig raten. Unsere Metriken messen, wo auf diesem Spektrum ein Modell liegt.

In dieser Lektion bauen wir zwei grundlegende Metriken von Grund auf: den Cross-Entropy-Loss (die Funktion, die wir während des Trainings minimieren) und die Perplexität (die daraus abgeleitete, intuitive Evaluationsmetrik). Dies sind nicht bloß abstrakte Formeln — sie sind der Kompass, der während des Pretrainings jede Entscheidung über Lernrate, Batch-Größe, Modellgröße und Trainingsdauer leitet.

Von Wahrscheinlichkeiten zum Loss: Die Cross-Entropy-Geschichte

Was das Modell tatsächlich ausgibt

Erinnern Sie sich, dass unser GPT-Modell mit einer linearen Projektion von der versteckten Dimension (d_model) auf die Vokabulargröße (vocab_size) endet. Für ein Vokabular von 50.257 Token (GPT-2) erzeugt jede Position einen Vektor mit 50.257 Zahlen, die Logits genannt werden. Das sind rohe, unnormalisierte Werte — jede beliebige reelle Zahl, positiv oder negativ.

Um Logits in Wahrscheinlichkeiten umzuwandeln, wenden wir die Softmax-Funktion an:

Softmax-Funktion

P(Token = i) = exp(zi) / ∑j=1V exp(zj)

Dies garantiert, dass alle Wahrscheinlichkeiten positiv sind und sich zu 1 summieren. Höhere Logits entsprechen höheren Wahrscheinlichkeiten. Softmax ist "weich" ("soft"), weil sie jedem Token eine gewisse Wahrscheinlichkeit zuweist, wobei die Verteilung umso spitzer wird, je größer die Unterschiede zwischen den Logits sind.

Die Cross-Entropy-Loss-Funktion

Angenommen, das Modell sagt für jeden Token eine Wahrscheinlichkeit P(Token = i) voraus, und der tatsächliche nächste Token ist Token t. Der Cross-Entropy-Loss misst, wie überrascht das Modell vom wahren Token war:

Cross-Entropy-Loss (einzelner Token)

L = −log P(Token = t)

Dies ist einfach die negative Log-Wahrscheinlichkeit der richtigen Antwort.

Warum diese Formel intuitiv Sinn ergibt:

  • Wahrscheinlichkeit 1,0 für den korrekten Token: L = −log(1,0) = 0. Perfekte Vorhersage, kein Loss.
  • Wahrscheinlichkeit 0,5: L = −log(0,5) ≈ 0,693. Ordentlich, aber unsicher.
  • Wahrscheinlichkeit 0,01: L = −log(0,01) ≈ 4,605. Sehr überrascht vom korrekten Token.
  • Wahrscheinlichkeit nähert sich 0 an: L → ∞. Katastrophal falsch.
Analogie: Der Wettervorhersager

Stellen Sie sich einen Wettervorhersager vor, der dem morgigen Wetter Wahrscheinlichkeiten zuweist. Sagt er "90 % Regenwahrscheinlichkeit" und es regnet, ist sein Loss niedrig (−log(0,9) ≈ 0,105). Sagt er "5 % Regenwahrscheinlichkeit" und es regnet, ist sein Loss sehr hoch (−log(0,05) ≈ 3,0). Cross-Entropy bestraft selbstsichere falsche Vorhersagen deutlich stärker als unsichere. Genau das wollen wir: Ein Modell, das sagt "Ich bin mir zu 99 % sicher, dass das nächste Wort 'Katze' ist", und sich dabei irrt, sollte eine hohe Strafe erhalten.

Der LogSoftmax-Trick für numerische Stabilität

In der Praxis berechnen wir niemals explizit die Softmax-Wahrscheinlichkeiten, um dann den Logarithmus zu nehmen. Stattdessen verwenden wir die Log-Softmax-Identität, die numerisch stabiler ist:

Log-Softmax (numerisch stabil)

log P(Token = i) = (zi − zmax) − log(∑j=1V exp(zj − zmax))

Indem wir vor der Exponentiation das maximale Logit subtrahieren, vermeiden wir die Berechnung von exp sehr großer Zahlen (was zu einem Überlauf gegen unendlich führen würde). Die Subtraktion hebt sich mathematisch auf, verhindert aber eine numerische Katastrophe.

Für eine vollständige Sequenz von T Token berechnen wir den Loss an jeder Position und mitteln ihn. Jeder Term misst, wie gut das Modell den Token an Position i anhand aller vorangehenden Token vorhergesagt hat:

Lseq = −(1/T) ∑i=1T log P(Tokeni | Token1, ..., Tokeni−1)

Python 

import numpy as np
np.random.seed(42)

# ============================================================
# Cross-Entropy Loss from Scratch
# ============================================================

def softmax(logits):
    """Compute softmax probabilities (numerically stable)."""
    shifted = logits - np.max(logits, axis=-1, keepdims=True)
    exp_vals = np.exp(shifted)
    return exp_vals / np.sum(exp_vals, axis=-1, keepdims=True)

def cross_entropy_loss(logits, targets):
    """
    Compute cross-entropy loss from logits and integer targets.

    logits: (batch_size, seq_len, vocab_size) - raw model outputs
    targets: (batch_size, seq_len) - correct next token IDs
    Returns: scalar average loss
    """
    batch_size, seq_len, vocab_size = logits.shape

    # Log-softmax (numerically stable)
    shifted = logits - np.max(logits, axis=-1, keepdims=True)
    log_sum_exp = np.log(np.sum(np.exp(shifted), axis=-1))
    log_probs = shifted - log_sum_exp[..., np.newaxis]

    # Extract log-probability of the correct token at each position
    batch_idx = np.arange(batch_size)[:, np.newaxis]
    seq_idx = np.arange(seq_len)[np.newaxis, :]
    target_log_probs = log_probs[batch_idx, seq_idx, targets]

    return -np.mean(target_log_probs)

# --- Demo: Three scenarios ---
vocab_size, seq_len, batch_size = 10, 5, 2
logits = np.random.randn(batch_size, seq_len, vocab_size)
targets = np.random.randint(0, vocab_size, (batch_size, seq_len))

loss = cross_entropy_loss(logits, targets)
print("=== Cross-Entropy Loss Demo ===")
print(f"Vocabulary size: {vocab_size} | Sequence length: {seq_len}")
print(f"Random model loss: {loss:.4f}")
print(f"Expected for random guessing: -log(1/{vocab_size}) = {-np.log(1/vocab_size):.4f}")
print()

# Near-perfect model: high logit for correct token
perfect = np.full((batch_size, seq_len, vocab_size), -10.0)
for b in range(batch_size):
    for t in range(seq_len):
        perfect[b, t, targets[b, t]] = 10.0
print(f"Near-perfect model loss: {cross_entropy_loss(perfect, targets):.6f}")
print("  (Close to 0: the model is confident about the right answers)")

# Deliberately wrong model: high logit for wrong tokens
wrong = np.full((batch_size, seq_len, vocab_size), 10.0)
for b in range(batch_size):
    for t in range(seq_len):
        wrong[b, t, targets[b, t]] = -10.0
print(f"Deliberately wrong loss: {cross_entropy_loss(wrong, targets):.4f}")
print("  (Very high: the model is confident about wrong answers)")

Perplexität: Den Loss intuitiv machen

Der Cross-Entropy-Loss ist die Zahl, die wir optimieren, aber sie ist schwer direkt zu interpretieren. Was bedeutet ein Loss von 3,2 wirklich? Ist das gut oder schlecht? An dieser Stelle kommt die Perplexität ins Spiel — sie wandelt den abstrakten Loss-Wert in etwas um, das man intuitiv erfassen kann.

Perplexität

PPL = exp(L)

wobei L der durchschnittliche Cross-Entropy-Loss pro Token ist. Die Perplexität stellt die effektive Anzahl von Token dar, zwischen denen das Modell bei jedem Schritt wählt. Hat ein Modell eine Perplexität von 100, bedeutet das, dass das Modell im Durchschnitt so unsicher ist, als würde es gleichverteilt zwischen 100 gleich wahrscheinlichen Token wählen.

Eine niedrigere Perplexität bedeutet immer ein besseres Modell. Hier sind einige Referenzwerte:

  • PPL = 1: Perfekte Vorhersage. Das Modell weiß immer genau, was als Nächstes kommt.
  • PPL = vocab_size (z. B. 50.257): Zufälliges Raten. Das Modell hat nichts gelernt.
  • GPT-2 Small: PPL ~35 auf WikiText-103 — Eingrenzung auf ~35 plausible nächste Token.
  • GPT-3 (175B): PPL ~20 auf ähnlichen Benchmarks.
  • State of the Art (2024-2025): Perplexitäten im niedrigen zweistelligen Bereich.
Analogie: Der Multiple-Choice-Test

Stellen Sie sich einen Test vor, bei dem jede Frage V Antwortmöglichkeiten hat. Die Perplexität sagt Ihnen die effektive Anzahl der Möglichkeiten, die das Modell für plausibel hält. Eine Perplexität von 5 bedeutet, dass das Modell die Auswahl auf etwa 5 plausible Möglichkeiten eingegrenzt hat, selbst wenn V 50.000 beträgt. Eine Perplexität von 50.000 bedeutet, dass alle Token gleich wahrscheinlich erscheinen — das Modell hat nichts über die Struktur der Sprache gelernt.

Warum sich die Perplexität ideal zum Vergleich von Modellen eignet

Die Perplexität besitzt mehrere Eigenschaften, die sie zur Standard-Evaluationsmetrik machen:

  1. Skaleninvariant: Eine PPL von 20 bedeutet dasselbe, unabhängig von Vokabular- oder Datensatzgröße.
  2. Multiplikativ: Eine Halbierung der Perplexität (z. B. von 40 auf 20) bedeutet, dass sich die Vorhersagegenauigkeit des Modells verdoppelt hat.
  3. Vergleichbar: Man kann die PPL zwischen Architekturen direkt vergleichen (gleiches Vokabular und gleicher Evaluationssatz).
  4. Niedriger ist besser: Einfache, eindeutige Interpretation.
Python 

import numpy as np
np.random.seed(42)

# ============================================================
# Perplexity: From Loss to Intuition
# ============================================================

def compute_perplexity(logits, targets):
    """Compute both cross-entropy loss and perplexity."""
    batch_size, seq_len, vocab_size = logits.shape
    shifted = logits - np.max(logits, axis=-1, keepdims=True)
    log_sum_exp = np.log(np.sum(np.exp(shifted), axis=-1))
    log_probs = shifted - log_sum_exp[..., np.newaxis]
    batch_idx = np.arange(batch_size)[:, np.newaxis]
    seq_idx = np.arange(seq_len)[np.newaxis, :]
    target_log_probs = log_probs[batch_idx, seq_idx, targets]
    avg_loss = -np.mean(target_log_probs)
    return avg_loss, np.exp(avg_loss)

# Simulate models at different quality levels

targets = np.random.randint(0, vocab_size, (batch_size, seq_len))

print()

print("-" * 75)

    ("Excellent",          0.1, 10.0),
]
for name, noise_scale, boost in configs:

    if boost > 0:

    loss, ppl = compute_perplexity(logits, targets)
    print(f"  {name:<20} {loss:>7.3f} {ppl:>11.1f}   Choosing among ~{ppl:.0f} tokens")

print()

print("(random guessing across 1000 tokens) toward single digits.")
print("Each improvement means the model is more 'certain' about what comes next.")

Trainings- vs. Validierungsloss: Overfitting erkennen

In der Praxis betrachten wir niemals nur eine einzelne Loss-Zahl. Wir berechnen den Loss auf zwei getrennten Datensätzen:

  • Trainingsloss: Berechnet auf Daten, die das Modell gesehen und aus denen es gelernt hat. Dieser sollte immer sinken.
  • Validierungsloss: Berechnet auf Daten, die das Modell nie gesehen hat. Er zeigt, ob das Modell allgemeine Muster lernt oder nur die Trainingsdaten auswendig lernt.

Das Overfitting-Signal

Die Beziehung zwischen Trainings- und Validierungsloss offenbart drei Trainingsregime:

  • Underfitting: Beide Losses sind hoch. Das Modell hat nicht genug gelernt. Training fortsetzen.
  • Gute Anpassung: Beide Losses sind niedrig und liegen nah beieinander. Das Modell hat verallgemeinerbare Muster gelernt.
  • Overfitting: Der Trainingsloss sinkt weiter, aber der Validierungsloss beginnt zu steigen. Das Modell lernt auswendig.

Die Lücke zwischen Validierungs- und Trainingsloss wird als Generalisierungslücke bezeichnet. Eine wachsende Lücke ist das eindeutigste Signal dafür, dass Overfitting eingesetzt hat.

Metriken auf Token-Ebene vs. auf Sequenz-Ebene

Es gibt eine wichtige Unterscheidung, die man verstehen sollte:

  • Metriken auf Token-Ebene (Loss, Perplexität pro Token): Werden während des Pretrainings verwendet. Sie liefern dem Optimierer ein glattes, differenzierbares Signal.
  • Metriken auf Sequenz-Ebene (BLEU, ROUGE, menschliche Bewertung): Bewerten vollständig generierte Sequenzen. Diese sind der Evaluation nachgelagerter Aufgaben nach dem Pretraining vorbehalten.
Python 

import numpy as np
np.random.seed(42)

# ============================================================
# Simulating Training vs Validation Loss Over Training
# ============================================================

epochs = np.arange(1, n_epochs + 1)

# Training loss: always decreasing (with noise)

# Validation loss: decreases, then increases (overfitting after epoch ~30)

print(f"\

for r_i, row in enumerate(grid):

Die Loss-Landschaft: Was der Optimierer sieht

Beim Training eines Modells navigiert der Optimierer durch eine hochdimensionale Loss-Landschaft — eine Oberfläche, bei der jeder Punkt einer bestimmten Menge von Modellgewichten entspricht und die Höhe dem Loss-Wert entspricht. Das Verständnis der wichtigsten Merkmale dieser Landschaft schafft entscheidende Intuition:

  • Globales Minimum: Der absolut niedrigste Punkt. Diesen zu finden ist für neuronale Netze im Allgemeinen unmöglich.
  • Lokale Minima: Punkte, die niedriger liegen als ihre unmittelbare Umgebung. Bei großen Modellen sind diese oft "gut genug" — Forschung zeigt, dass sie tendenziell ähnliche Loss-Werte aufweisen.
  • Sattelpunkte: Minima in manchen Richtungen, Maxima in anderen. In hohen Dimensionen häufiger als lokale Minima und können das Training erheblich verlangsamen.
  • Flache Regionen (Plateaus): Große Bereiche, in denen sich der Loss kaum verändert. Die Gradienten sind nahe null, wodurch der Fortschritt quälend langsam wird.

Forschung hat gezeigt, dass größere Modelle tendenziell glattere, besser handhabbare Landschaften mit weniger problematischen lokalen Minima aufweisen. Das ist einer der Gründe, warum eine Vergrößerung der Modellgröße das Training oft einfacher statt schwieriger macht — ein kontraintuitiver, aber gut dokumentierter Befund.

Praktische Überlegungen

Häufige Fallstricke bei der Loss-Berechnung

Fallstrick 1: Numerischer Überlauf in Softmax

Ohne den Trick der Maximum-Subtraktion ist exp(1000) = ∞ in Gleitkommadarstellung. Subtrahieren Sie vor der Exponentiation stets das maximale Logit. Dies ist mathematisch äquivalent, aber numerisch sicher.

Fallstrick 2: Logarithmus von Null

Wenn eine Softmax-Wahrscheinlichkeit genau auf 0 unterläuft, ist log(0) = −∞. Fügen Sie entweder ein winziges Epsilon hinzu (log(probs + 1e-10)), oder verwenden Sie noch besser direkt die Log-Softmax-Formulierung, die dieses Problem vollständig vermeidet.

Fallstrick 3: Padding-Token ignorieren

Wenn Sequenzen unterschiedliche Längen haben und aufgefüllt (gepaddet) werden, dürfen Padding-Positionen nicht in den Loss einbezogen werden. Verwenden Sie eine Loss-Maske, die Padding-Beiträge auf null setzt. Andernfalls verschwendet das Modell Kapazität darauf, bedeutungslose Padding-Symbole vorherzusagen.

Welche Loss-Werte zu erwarten sind

  • Bei der Initialisierung (zufällige Gewichte): Loss ≈ log(vocab_size). Für vocab=50.257: ~10,8
  • Nach wenigen Schritten: Fällt rasch auf 7-8, während das Modell Token-Häufigkeiten lernt
  • Nach umfangreichem Training: 3-4 für GPT-2-Skala auf Webtext
  • Vollständig konvergiertes GPT-2: Loss ~3,0-3,5 (Perplexität 20-33)
  • Große Modelle (175B+): Loss ~2,5-3,0 (Perplexität 12-20)
Plausibilitätsprüfung: Weicht Ihr anfänglicher Loss deutlich von log(vocab_size) ab, stimmt etwas mit der Initialisierung Ihres Modells oder der Loss-Berechnung nicht. Dies ist die allererste Prüfung, die jeder Praktiker zu Beginn eines Trainingslaufs durchführt.

Zusammenfassung: Das Evaluations-Toolkit

In dieser Lektion haben wir das vollständige Evaluations-Toolkit für das Pretraining von Sprachmodellen aufgebaut:

  1. Cross-Entropy-Loss misst die negative Log-Wahrscheinlichkeit des korrekten nächsten Tokens, gemittelt über alle Positionen. Es ist die Loss-Funktion, die wir während des Trainings minimieren.
  2. Perplexität = exp(Loss) — die effektive Anzahl von Token, zwischen denen das Modell "wählt". Eine Perplexität von 20 bedeutet, dass das Modell den nächsten Token auf etwa 20 plausible Kandidaten eingrenzt.
  3. Trainings- vs. Validierungsloss deckt Overfitting auf, wenn die Generalisierungslücke zu wachsen beginnt.
  4. Die Loss-Landschaft liefert geometrische Intuition darüber, wodurch sich der Optimierer bewegt und warum größere Modelle tendenziell leichter zu trainieren sind.

Mit diesen Metriken zur Hand sind wir bereit, die eigentliche Trainingsschleife zu bauen. In der nächsten Lektion konstruieren wir den DataLoader, der dem Modell Text zuführt, und implementieren die vollständige Pretraining-Schleife.

Selbsttest: Zentrale Erkenntnis

Wenn ein Forscher sagt "wir haben eine Perplexität von 15,2 auf WikiText-103 erreicht", was genau sagt Ihnen diese Zahl über das Modell? Wie würden Sie die Validierungsperplexität während des Trainings nutzen, um zu entscheiden, wann Sie Ihre Strategie ändern sollten? Warum gelten diese beiden Metriken als die "Sprache des Pretrainings"?
